intended_object: The canonical ring isomorphism (S^{(n)})_{(f)} ≅ S_{(f)} for n > 0, where S is an ℕ-graded commutative ring, S^{(n)} = ⊕_j S_{nj} is its n-th Veronese ring and f is homogeneous of degree j in S^{(n)} (so of degree nj in S). It identifies the degree-zero homogeneous localizations, i.e. the affine charts D₊(f) of Proj S^{(n)} and Proj S. Inferred from the docstring, the name and its use in `isIso_forward` / `schemeIso`.
explanation:
The body builds the ring equivalence from the degree-multiplying map `Away.mapDegreeMul`, which sends a/f^k to ι(a)/ι(f)^k, where ι : S^{(n)} → S is the inclusion. It shows this map is bijective. Injectivity comes from ι being injective when n > 0, which carries over to the localizations. Surjectivity holds because any numerator of degree k·nj in S lies in S_{n(kj)}, which is the degree-kj component of the Veronese ring. This is exactly the standard isomorphism (S^{(n)})_{(f)} ≅ S_{(f)}.

The hypotheses are the right ones. The condition n > 0 is genuinely needed: for n = 0, ι is not injective. The degree j may be any natural number, including 0. The definition does not assume f is a non-zero-divisor or that f is not nilpotent, which is what the docstring means by "nilpotent-safe".

The setting (ℕ-graded rings, homogeneous localization `Away`) is the one in which Mathlib defines Proj, so the generality is natural. Mathlib has no Veronese construction (grepping for "Veronese" finds nothing), so there is no Mathlib counterpart. The definition is a canonical mathematical isomorphism used as a building block for Proj S ≅ Proj S^{(n)}, and it is correctly formalized.
